~~~text
\hypertarget{pd15:investment}{%
\chapter{When a bank experiment becomes worth its
cost}\label{pd15:investment}}

\hypertarget{proposal-acceptance-and-later-qualification}{%
\section{The evidence needed before investing}\label{proposal-acceptance-and-later-qualification}}

The investment decision requires a comparison of feasible alternatives,
their costs and the evidence for their expected benefits. Reproducible
public and simulated studies can support that comparison within their
stated assumptions. A restricted result may justify a narrow prototype
while leaving broader research questions unresolved.

Public evidence informs three choices: which existing methods to reuse,
where language assistance is useful, and how analysts should conduct a
reproducible study. A dataset can reveal a timing error or support a
controlled comparison without settling every question about those choices.

Later bank qualification asks a different question: do the assumptions,
precision, workflows and economics hold for a specific institution? That
stage may need genuine offer histories, logging information, independent
labels, owner-reviewed semantics, production constraints and prospective
outcomes. The relevant input should be requested only for the capability
and target population under test. An internal bank pilot is not required
to demonstrate that the proposal has a reproducible public baseline and
a sensible experiment design.

\hypertarget{a-value-of-information-decision}{%
\section{A value-of-information
decision}\label{a-value-of-information-decision}}

Let \(d\in\{\text{stop},\text{build},\text{pilot}\}\) denote an
investment choice, \(\theta\) unresolved technical and economic
conditions, and \(U(d,\theta)\) its net value. Let \(E\) denote current
public/prototype evidence and \(Z\) the possible result of a proposed
experiment. A planning expression for the expected value of sample
information is

\[
\operatorname{EVSI}
=\mathbb E_{Z\mid E}\!\left[\max_d\mathbb E\{U(d,\theta)\mid E,Z\}\right]
-\max_d\mathbb E\{U(d,\theta)\mid E\}.
\]

An experiment merits consideration when its expected decision
improvement exceeds its full incremental cost, including data
preparation, customer burden where relevant, security review, labeling,
analyst time and opportunity cost. This is a project decision framework,
not an empirically estimated ROI. Where a probability model for
\(\theta\) is unjustified, use a scenario table and sensitivity bounds
instead of a precise-looking EVSI number.

A simple illustrative calculation shows the sequencing. Suppose, purely
for planning, a small bank study costing 20,000 could avert an
unsuitable 200,000 build in 20\% of scenarios, with no other benefits or
costs. Its gross avoided-spend value would be 40,000 and its net would
be 20,000 under those assumptions. If the study changes the build
decision in only 2\% of scenarios, the same gross value is 4,000 and it
is not justified on that ground. These are stipulated arithmetic
examples, not quotations, bank probabilities or forecasts.

The decision should identify the uncertainty that matters. If a public
benchmark shows repeated action-clock mistakes, improve the formulation
layer before requesting confidential data. If a correct estimator is too
slow on modest data, fix or replace it before commissioning a platform
pilot. If all plausible effects lead to the same action, a costly
precision improvement may have little value. If policy value reverses
when a missing hardship variable is plausible, a carefully scoped bank
measurement study can have high value even when the public-data
implementation is technically sound.

\hypertarget{conditions-for-moving-to-expensive-evidence}{%
\section{Conditions for moving to expensive
evidence}\label{conditions-for-moving-to-expensive-evidence}}

An actionable next-experiment recommendation specifies the proposed
intervention, target population, candidate baseline, decision-loss
threshold and the smallest information addition that could alter the
decision. It also states an explicit stop or redesign outcome. A bank
experiment should not be recommended merely to fill a missing-evidence
cell.

For funding, the missing addition may be time-stamped offers and an
assignment mechanism, not more aggregate deposits. For servicing, it may
be feasible-action and hardship information at each decision time. For
discovery, it may be one feasible intervention that distinguishes
competing graphs. For observation construction, it may be a
representative independently resolved sample of uncertain identities
with known inclusion probabilities. Public data help design each
measurement and estimate its computational burden, while the bank
supplies the later population-specific truth.

Authentic institutional approval, independent acceptance, actual
workflow prices and production service levels remain future
qualification requirements. A proposal can be complete without them. It
cannot honestly claim those outcomes without obtaining them.

\hypertarget{remaining-survey-and-prototype-gaps}{%
\section{Remaining survey and prototype
gaps}\label{remaining-survey-and-prototype-gaps}}

The survey has established a usable portfolio and a concrete public-data
acquisition/profile, not six executed new studies. Current-source web
snapshots still need exact data-file vintages for future analyses.
Several benchmark datasets need data-specific rights checks. Mortgage
histories require registration and use review; the HMDA publication
endpoint was inaccessible in this run. The Criteo license is a material
constraint for a commercial proposal. These affect individual options;
project-generated alternatives and the already local public data keep
the prototype work moving.

No inspected public financial source supplies the complete logged bank
servicing action process or independent real-bank linkage truth. That
finding is limited to the surveyed sources. It calls for transparent
semi-synthetic experiments now and a justified targeted measurement
later, rather than a claim of impossibility. Public reasoning benchmarks
also cannot establish a live agent's quality without an actual
controlled run, nor resolve the business owner's normative choice of
outcome and feasible intervention.

Finally, public data do not repair the open mathematical arguments for
persistent dependence, hidden states, graph-equivalence effect sets or
arbitrary learning procedures. Those questions remain scoped research
obligations. The proposal can present negative findings and restricted
supported regimes, compare alternatives and describe what evidence would
change the recommendation. That is a strong proposal standard without
pretending that an accepted bank product already exists.
~~~

~~~text
\section{Estimated policies, missing rewards and decision uncertainty}
Chapters~\ref{gap29:servicing} and \ref{gap29:policy-uncertainty} carry the
policy question into fitted data. They use a separate three-decision economy,
with continuous states and rewards already net of the stipulated action cost.
Those reward units are not the pounds in this two-contact example. Whole
customers, rather than isolated rows, supply the sampling units. A separate
training sample chooses the policy; evaluation and resampling hold that
selected policy fixed.

The fitted comparison is informative precisely because it can fail.
Under its maintained state and observation model, improvement coverage is
94\% with an average interval width of 0.711 reward units. Future-dependent
dropout reduces coverage to 6\%; omitting a state predictor reduces it to
61\%. These observed fractions have Monte Carlo uncertainty, reported in
the study. They demonstrate that resampling an estimated model does not
repair an invalid observation assumption.

The financial interpretation follows the reward definition. Where costs are
already subtracted, subtracting contact cost again would double-count it.
~~~

~~~text
\chapter{From an offer effect to annual contribution}
\label{rewrite:deposit}
\input{writing-repair/2026-10-29/src/ec8ce8fc42140471.tex}

\section{Fix the intervention before estimating its value}
The preceding accounting calculation defines the question for the first
complete study. Let $Z_i$ denote assignment of the offer to eligible household
$i$, $R_i$ its delivery, $D_i$ acceptance, and $r_i$ the paid annual rate.
These variables describe successive events, not synonyms. Let $B_i(z)$ be
the household's average eligible deposit balance over the following year under
assignment $z$, and let $C_i(z)$ be contribution over that same year. For a
population fixed before assignment, the policy targets are
\[
 \tau_B=\E[B_i(1)-B_i(0)],\qquad
 \tau_C=\E[C_i(1)-C_i(0)].
\]
A statement about the effect among acceptors generally answers neither target.
Acceptance can depend on intentions that also determine balances. Dividing an
assignment effect by an acceptance rate additionally requires an instrumental
variable argument and changes the population to the relevant compliers; the
derivation and restrictions are in Chapter~\ref{r3:instruments}.

Here the constructed design makes a narrower intervention explicit. Every
assigned offer is delivered, and assignment automatically reprices the eligible
balance for one year. Thus $R=Z$ and the price rule is $r=r_0+Z\Delta r$;
acceptance does not gate the payment. A voluntary activation campaign would
need a different expense equation. Assume no interference across households,
no lost outcomes, and unchanged funding margin and direct cost. If the
expected no-offer balance is $B_0$, the incremental expected contribution is
\begin{equation}
 \tau_C=(m-\Delta r)\tau_B-\Delta r B_0-c.
 \label{rewrite:value-map}
\end{equation}
To obtain this expression, subtract $mB_i(0)$ from
$(m-\Delta r)B_i(1)-c$, then take expectations. It charges the rate
increase on the balance that would have remained without the intervention.
The familiar accounting shortcut is justified by this particular price rule.
It would overcharge a campaign that paid only newly acquired funds and would
misdescribe a campaign whose delivery itself failed.

\section{A deliberately transparent assignment design}
The example has two equally weighted customer strata, $X=0,1$. Assignment is
independent of potential balances within each stratum, with probabilities
$e_0=0.5$ and $e_1=0.1$. Both strata have mean no-offer balance
\pounds10,000. The stipulated balance effects are $b_0=0$ and $b_1=2,400$,
with independent normal household noise of standard deviation \pounds400.
These are generated customers. In particular, the independence and normal
law are supplied by construction and have not been inferred from bank data.

Consistency, assignment exchangeability within $X$, and positive assignment
probabilities give
\[
 \tau_B=\sum_{x=0}^1 w_x
   \{\E[B\mid Z=1,X=x]-\E[B\mid Z=0,X=x]\},
 \qquad w_0=w_1=\tfrac12.
\]
The two weights describe the target population, not the observed distribution
of offered customers. The population contrast is therefore \pounds1,200.
A saturated cell-mean estimator uses the same weights. It is a useful first
implementation because every contribution to the answer can be inspected;
with two strata there is no need to learn a complex outcome surface.

A constant residual projection gives a different average when effects vary.
Its weights are proportional to $w_xe_x(1-e_x)$, giving weight
$0.09/(0.25+0.09)$ to the high-benefit stratum and a population coefficient
of about \pounds635.29. That is a valid projection target. Calling it the
equal-stratum population effect would change the financial answer from
positive \pounds3 to about negative \pounds12.53. Chapter~\ref{scisyn:evidence}
retains the separately executed repeated experiments on this target error
and on sparse support. The current single sample demonstrates the full report;
it does not add another calibration experiment.

\section{Carry uncertainty through the expense equation}
Write $n_{xa}$, $\bar B_{xa}$ and $s_{xa}$ for the count, mean and sample
standard deviation of each observed cell. For a total error allowance
$\alpha=0.05$, construct four mean intervals
\[
 I_{xa}=\bar B_{xa}\ \pm\
 t_{n_{xa}-1,1-\alpha/8}\frac{s_{xa}}{\sqrt{n_{xa}}}.
\]
Each interval has conditional noncoverage $\alpha/4$ under its normal
independent sampling law. The union bound implies simultaneous coverage
at least $1-\alpha$, without assuming independence among the four interval
events. Conditioning on the observed assignment counts is legitimate here
because assignment is independent of the outcome errors within strata.
A cell with fewer than two observations returns unsupported rather than a
zero standard error.

If $h_{xa}$ denotes a cell half-width, interval arithmetic yields
\[
 \widehat\tau_B=\tfrac12(\bar B_{01}-\bar B_{00})+
                     \tfrac12(\bar B_{11}-\bar B_{10}),\qquad
 I_B=\widehat\tau_B\ \pm\ \tfrac12\sum_{x,a}h_{xa}.
\]
This construction permits different cell variances. It is conservative and
can become too wide to guide action. The earlier generated study shows why
a narrower pooled interval needs an additional common-variance assumption.
A shared service should expose that tradeoff, not silently choose the
narrower result. The present argument does not justify the Student intervals
under heavy tails, common calendar shocks or dependent households.

With $m=0.03$, $\Delta r=0.0025$, $B_0=10,000$ and $c=5$, equation
\eqref{rewrite:value-map} is increasing in $\tau_B$. Its endpoints
therefore transform directly: $I_C=0.0275 I_B-30$. Uncertainty in these

\bottomrule

\end{center}
The four cells contain 2,039 unoffered and 1,961 offered households in the

model and expense rule. Its margin is small: an additional certain expense

\end{lstlisting}
The callable result and a separate command-line process agree exactly in
the retained execution. The generated data, code, seed and numerical results
are supplied with the study. This is a specific estimator implemented for
the example; it is not evidence that an external causal package was qualified.

The existing MCP walkthrough separately establishes graph syntax, conditional
adjustment, information-date checks and refusal of a dependent sampling law
through that route. It does not expose this new estimator as an MCP operation.
Chapter~\ref{scisyn:investment} gives the observed requests and the initial
timeout as well as the successful retry. Combining those two observations
into a claim of a completed MCP financial analysis would overstate the work.
A future adapter must carry the complete report, including assumptions and
unsupported outcomes, before that claim becomes available.

\section{From the household offer to broader funding evidence}
Two extensions show what this transparent report leaves to be learned.
Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} estimates an assignment contrast from the retained
public experiment, compares adjusted and unadjusted estimators, examines
influence, and subtracts an explicit cost. Its earnings units and population
are different from the deposit account: the exercise tests an inferential
and reporting route, not transport of an earnings effect into bank balances.
Chapter~\ref{gap29:funding} follows institutions rather than households and
asks whether fixed effects can repair a misassigned outcome. They cannot
recover the institution's identity merely by absorbing a persistent level.
The structural funding and calendar arguments explain the additional shock
and dependence assumptions needed for that journey.

For the offer study, the next source of information is assignment support and
correct household aggregation; for the institutional panel it is a coherent
exposure and outcome history. A bank cannot substitute a successful estimate
in one of these populations for the missing design evidence in the other.
The shared report can preserve both questions without pretending they have
the same estimator or sampling law.

\chapter{Servicing decisions change the next decision's information}
\label{rewrite:servicing}

A servicing policy chooses whether to contact a borrower at two dates. Let
$A_0,A_1$ be contact decisions, $L_0$ baseline borrower state and $L_1$ the
state observed between contacts. For this constructed example, $Y$ is
gross contribution in pounds over the two-period horizon, excluding contact
cost. The policy comparison is sustained contact versus no contact, not
the regression coefficient of one contact conditional on every later event.

The exact law developed in Chapter~\ref{r3:longitudinal} is
\begin{align*}
 P(L_0=1)&=0.5,\\
 P(A_0=1\mid L_0)&=0.2+0.6L_0,\\
 P(L_1=1\mid L_0,A_0)&=0.1+0.5L_0+0.2A_0,\\
 P(A_1=1\mid H_1)&=0.15+0.5L_1+0.1A_0,\\
 Y&=20+3A_0+4A_1+10L_1+6L_0.
\end{align*}
Here $H_1=(L_0,A_0,L_1)$ is the history available for the second action.
Independent innovations implement these kernels. The actions have support
for every possible history, and the example has no hidden confounding.
Consequently, replacing both action kernels with a specified policy and
retaining the state-transition law identifies its mean. This is the
g-formula developed from sequential exchangeability in the retained chapter
and its primary treatment. \citep[Chapter 21]{hernan2020}

\section{Average the state produced by each policy}
For a constant policy $a$, the mean intermediate state is
$\E[L_1(a)]=0.1+0.5(0.5)+0.2a=0.35+0.2a$. Hence
\[
 \psi(a)=20+7a+10(0.35+0.2a)+6(0.5)=26.5+9a.
\]
The gross means are \pounds26.50 and \pounds35.50. At a stipulated
\pounds2 per contact, the net contrast is $9-2(2)=\pounds5$.
The reported exact enumeration independently averages the finite state law
and reweights the observed action paths; both recover the same two means.
There is no finite-sample confidence claim in this calculation.

A regression of $Y$ on all four variables correctly recovers action
coefficients 3 and 4. Their sum misses the extra $10(0.2)=2$ contributed
through the change in $L_1$. Removing $L_1$ from the second-stage regression
does not repair the analysis: the historical second action depends on it.
The calculation therefore distinguishes a fitted conditional equation from
the policy mean obtained by averaging that equation over policy-specific
histories. The distinction changes net value from an erroneous \pounds3
to \pounds5 even in this noise-free conditional outcome model.

\section{What changes when the law must be learned}
In an observed study, the kernels and outcome regressions are estimated.
G-computation substitutes fitted transition and outcome laws and averages
under the target policy. Reweighting instead uses ratios of target to
historical action probabilities. Doubly robust constructions combine these
ideas; their longitudinal scores, nuisance restrictions and remainders are
derived in Chapter~\ref{r3:longitudinal}, rather than assumed from their
name. None removes the requirement that the historical records include
the information responsible for action selection.

For sustained contact, a useful diagnostic is the count and weight
distribution of complete histories supporting that policy. Many borrower
rows do not guarantee enough such histories. A policy learned by maximizing
the same estimated value must be evaluated with the additional selection
uncertainty or an honest evaluation sample. An outcome law conditional on
a hidden state introduces another identification problem; a well-fitting
state-space model does not establish that its intervention meaning is correct.

The product implication is to begin with a fixed, short-horizon policy and
observable histories, retaining a direct g-computation and a weighting
comparison. If support is inadequate or an important action determinant is
unrecorded, changing the collection or trial design is more informative than
adding a flexible learner. The positive \pounds5 example explains the
accounting; it does not establish a real contact policy's benefit.

\section{Estimated policies, missing rewards and decision uncertainty}
Chapters~\ref{gap29:servicing} and \ref{gap29:policy-uncertainty} carry the
policy question into fitted data. They use a separate three-decision economy,
with continuous states and rewards already net of the stipulated action cost.
Those reward units are not the pounds in this two-contact example. Whole
customers, rather than isolated rows, supply the sampling units. A separate
training sample chooses the policy; evaluation and resampling hold that
selected policy fixed.

The fitted comparison is informative precisely because it can fail.
Under its maintained state and observation model, improvement coverage is
94\% with an average interval width of 0.711 reward units. Future-dependent
dropout reduces coverage to 6\%; omitting a state predictor reduces it to
61\%. These observed fractions have Monte Carlo uncertainty, reported in
the study. They demonstrate that resampling an estimated model does not
repair an invalid observation assumption.

The financial interpretation follows the reward definition. Where costs are
already subtracted, subtracting contact cost again would double-count it.
Where a bank's reward law and initial distribution must also be estimated,
the supplied-law components of the generated comparison cannot be treated
as known. Outcome follow-up, action support and measured decision history
therefore determine whether its narrower uncertainty can be useful.

\chapter{A learned graph can leave the pricing decision unresolved}
\label{rewrite:discovery}

Suppose $X$ measures a proposed rate change in percentage points, $M$ an
intermediate market quantity and $Y$ gross funding contribution in thousands
of pounds. The units and coefficients in this section are authored for the
example. Consider the centered Gaussian observational covariance
\[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&0.6&0.48\\0.6&1.36&1.088\\0.48&1.088&1.8704
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The law satisfies $X\perp Y\mid M$. A chain $X\to M\to Y$, a
fork $X\leftarrow M\to Y$, and a reverse chain $X\leftarrow M\leftarrow Y$
can all reproduce it using independent Gaussian errors.

For the first chain, take $M=0.6X+\varepsilon_M$ and
$Y=0.8M+\varepsilon_Y$, with variances $\Var(X)=1$,
$\Var(\varepsilon_M)=1$ and $\Var(\varepsilon_Y)=1$. The intervention
slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $0.6(0.8)=0.48$. For the fork, take
$\Var(M)=1.36$, $X=(0.6/1.36)M+\eta_X$, and $Y=0.8M+\eta_Y$,
with residual variances $1-0.6^2/1.36$ and $1$. The resulting covariance
is the same, but intervening on $X$ has zero effect on $Y$. The reverse
chain uses the corresponding conditional regression coefficients and also
has zero effect. The numerical check reconstructs all three covariance
matrices and verifies positive residual variances.

\section{Keep the causal ambiguity in the financial report}
Within this specified three-model family, the slope set is $\{0,0.48\}$.
At a quarter-point intervention and a stipulated \pounds60 action cost,
net value is
\[
 1000(0.25)\{0,0.48\}-60=\{-60,60\}
 \quad\hbox{pounds}.
\]
There is no sign-robust recommendation across the retained explanations.
Returning the slope from the forward chain alone would hide the unresolved
orientation that determines the action. A probability for each graph would
require additional justified modelling; equal probabilities are not supplied
by observational equivalence. Nor should the discrete set be called a
confidence interval. It represents identification ambiguity even if the
covariance is known exactly.

The example's finite graph family and linear Gaussian law are restrictions.
They do not describe every model compatible with arbitrary banking records.
When the covariance and graph class are estimated, uncertainty must cover
both the observed law and the retained models before mapping them to effects.
An edge bootstrap conditional on one chosen graph does not supply that
combined guarantee. The foundations and detailed temporal-discovery
comparisons retain the arguments for unresolved orientations, latent causes
and class-to-effect propagation.

For a bank, useful additional information could be a defensible ordering
that excludes two orientations, a valid instrument, or an intervention on
$X$. The cost of obtaining that information should be compared with the
consequence of a mistaken action. More precise estimation of this same
covariance cannot distinguish these three laws. The proposed service should
therefore preserve a class or explicit refusal and ask what would narrow it,
instead of completing arrows solely to make a diagram look decisive.

\section{From a known covariance to estimated effect sets}
Chapter~\ref{exec13:temporal-region} supplies the next inferential step under
a restricted stationary Gaussian time-series model. It constructs a region
jointly over the observed covariance, a continuous unknown common lag and a
declared family of causal models, then maps that region to effects. The
coverage argument keeps the true model and observed-law uncertainty together;
it does not condition on an orientation chosen for convenience. The chapter
also shows what a direct intervention can add.

This is a developed restricted construction, not an executed general
bank-discovery pipeline. The maintained graph family, scalar lag and
innovation law must be defensible before applying it. An unrestricted latent
model may leave the whole line admissible. In the opening pricing example,
the narrower set already contains opposite net values, so a more elaborate
estimator is useful only if its information or restrictions can resolve a
consequential ambiguity. A labelled whole-line result can be the correct
answer to a well-defined question.

\chapter{Correcting records can change the action}
\label{rewrite:observation}

A treatment record is a measurement of an event. Let $A$ be true randomized
receipt, $W$ recorded receipt and $Y$ gross contribution in pounds at a
fixed horizon. In this separate finite example, $P(A=0)=P(A=1)=1/2$
and $\E[Y\mid A=0]=100$, $\E[Y\mid A=1]=140$. Receipt is
randomized by construction; correcting its record would not establish
randomization in an observational campaign.

Suppose misclassification is nondifferential with a known matrix
\[
 K=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad K_{wa}=P(W=w\mid A=a,Y).
\]
Writing $p_a=P(A=a)$ and $q_a=\E[Y\mathbf1(A=a)]$, the recorded
shares and outcome moments obey
\[
 p_W=Kp_A=(0.55,0.45)' ,\qquad q_W=Kq_A=(59,61)' .
\]
Thus the recorded contrast is $61/0.45-59/0.55=28.2828\ldots$.
The matrix has determinant $0.7$, so its inverse recovers
$p_A=(0.5,0.5)'$ and $q_A=(50,70)'$, giving the true contrast
$70/0.5-50/0.5=40$. This is the moment version of the joint-law
argument in Chapter~\ref{r3:observation}. It is checked by direct
multiplication and solution, with no estimated audit law.

\section{The value of knowing the observation law}
At a stipulated action cost of \pounds35, the recorded comparison gives
net value about $-\pounds6.72$, whereas the corrected contrast gives
\pounds5. That reversal is conditional on the known error law. If an
identity matrix and the displayed matrix both remain admissible, the same
recorded shares and moments are compatible with different latent effects
and opposite recommendations. Reporting only the corrected number would
replace measurement uncertainty with a convenient assumption.

In a real validation sample, estimating $K$ would add uncertainty. The audit
must identify true receipt and represent the relevant customers and periods;
a classifier's own label is not an external truth measurement. Near-singular
matrices amplify error, and a singular matrix destroys recoverable information.
The retained chapter gives the symmetric-error example where receipt becomes
uninformative. More rows with the same deficient measurement law do not
restore its rank.

Entity linkage poses a related but distinct problem. A household may hold
several accounts, and a mistaken join can change both its treatment and its
outcome. Correctness counts alone may fail to identify the needed contrast;
the detailed linkage studies and their adverse results remain in this book.
The next useful observation is a correctly sampled, truthful linked history
when that is what the estimand requires, not merely a higher aggregate match
score. Likewise, event time, availability time and revision time must remain
separate when constructing a prospective decision view.

The four journeys now imply a common requirement for the proposed service.
It must keep the economic target and the information that identifies it
attached to the numerical result. Their statistical procedures remain
different: stratified assignment contrasts, sequential policy averaging,
model-set propagation and observation-law inversion. The next chapters
develop those differences before the software and investment synthesis chooses
which ones are ready for a bounded comparison.
~~~

~~~text
\section{Fix the intervention before estimating its value}
The preceding accounting calculation defines the question for the first
complete study. Let $Z_i$ denote assignment of the offer to eligible household
$i$, $R_i$ its delivery, $D_i$ acceptance, and $r_i$ the paid annual rate.
These variables describe successive events, not synonyms. Let $B_i(z)$ be
the household's average eligible deposit balance over the following year under
assignment $z$, and let $C_i(z)$ be contribution over that same year. For a
population fixed before assignment, the policy targets are
\[
 \tau_B=\E[B_i(1)-B_i(0)],\qquad
 \tau_C=\E[C_i(1)-C_i(0)].
\]
A statement about the effect among acceptors generally answers neither target.
Acceptance can depend on intentions that also determine balances. Dividing an
assignment effect by an acceptance rate additionally requires an instrumental
variable argument and changes the population to the relevant compliers; the
derivation and restrictions are in Chapter~\ref{r3:instruments}.

Here the constructed design makes a narrower intervention explicit. Every
assigned offer is delivered, and assignment automatically reprices the eligible
balance for one year. Thus $R=Z$ and the price rule is $r=r_0+Z\Delta r$;
acceptance does not gate the payment. A voluntary activation campaign would
need a different expense equation. Assume no interference across households,
no lost outcomes, and unchanged funding margin and direct cost. If the
expected no-offer balance is $B_0$, the incremental expected contribution is
\begin{equation}
 \tau_C=(m-\Delta r)\tau_B-\Delta r B_0-c.
 \label{rewrite:value-map}
\end{equation}
To obtain this expression, subtract $mB_i(0)$ from
$(m-\Delta r)B_i(1)-c$, then take expectations. It charges the rate
increase on the balance that would have remained without the intervention.
The familiar accounting shortcut is justified by this particular price rule.
It would overcharge a campaign that paid only newly acquired funds and would
misdescribe a campaign whose delivery itself failed.

\section{A deliberately transparent assignment design}
The example has two equally weighted customer strata, $X=0,1$. Assignment is
independent of potential balances within each stratum, with probabilities
$e_0=0.5$ and $e_1=0.1$. Both strata have mean no-offer balance
\pounds10,000. The stipulated balance effects are $b_0=0$ and $b_1=2,400$,
with independent normal household noise of standard deviation \pounds400.
These are generated customers. In particular, the independence and normal
law are supplied by construction and have not been inferred from bank data.

Consistency, assignment exchangeability within $X$, and positive assignment
probabilities give
\[

   \{\E[B\mid Z=1,X=x]-\E[B\mid Z=0,X=x]\},

\]
The two weights describe the target population, not the observed distribution
of offered customers. The population contrast is therefore \pounds1,200.

 \end{pmatrix}.

The law satisfies $X\perp Y\mid M$. A chain $X\to M\to Y$, a
fork $X\leftarrow M\to Y$, and a reverse chain $X\leftarrow M\leftarrow Y$
can all reproduce it using independent Gaussian errors.

For the first chain, take $M=0.6X+\varepsilon_M$ and
$Y=0.8M+\varepsilon_Y$, with variances $\Var(X)=1$,
$\Var(\varepsilon_M)=1$ and $\Var(\varepsilon_Y)=1$. The intervention
slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $0.6(0.8)=0.48$. For the fork, take
$\Var(M)=1.36$, $X=(0.6/1.36)M+\eta_X$, and $Y=0.8M+\eta_Y$,
with residual variances $1-0.6^2/1.36$ and $1$. The resulting covariance
is the same, but intervening on $X$ has zero effect on $Y$. The reverse
chain uses the corresponding conditional regression coefficients and also
has zero effect. The numerical check reconstructs all three covariance
matrices and verifies positive residual variances.

\section{Keep the causal ambiguity in the financial report}
Within this specified three-model family, the slope set is $\{0,0.48\}$.
At a quarter-point intervention and a stipulated \pounds60 action cost,
net value is
\[
 1000(0.25)\{0,0.48\}-60=\{-60,60\}
 \quad\hbox{pounds}.
\]
There is no sign-robust recommendation across the retained explanations.
Returning the slope from the forward chain alone would hide the unresolved
orientation that determines the action. A probability for each graph would
require additional justified modelling; equal probabilities are not supplied
by observational equivalence. Nor should the discrete set be called a
confidence interval. It represents identification ambiguity even if the
covariance is known exactly.

The example's finite graph family and linear Gaussian law are restrictions.
They do not describe every model compatible with arbitrary banking records.
When the covariance and graph class are estimated, uncertainty must cover
both the observed law and the retained models before mapping them to effects.
An edge bootstrap conditional on one chosen graph does not supply that
combined guarantee. The foundations and detailed temporal-discovery
comparisons retain the arguments for unresolved orientations, latent causes
and class-to-effect propagation.

For a bank, useful additional information could be a defensible ordering
that excludes two orientations, a valid instrument, or an intervention on
$X$. The cost of obtaining that information should be compared with the
consequence of a mistaken action. More precise estimation of this same
covariance cannot distinguish these three laws. The proposed service should
therefore preserve a class or explicit refusal and ask what would narrow it,
instead of completing arrows solely to make a diagram look decisive.

\section{From a known covariance to estimated effect sets}
Chapter~\ref{exec13:temporal-region} supplies the next inferential step under
a restricted stationary Gaussian time-series model. It constructs a region
jointly over the observed covariance, a continuous unknown common lag and a
declared family of causal models, then maps that region to effects. The
coverage argument keeps the true model and observed-law uncertainty together;
it does not condition on an orientation chosen for convenience. The chapter
also shows what a direct intervention can add.

This is a developed restricted construction, not an executed general
bank-discovery pipeline. The maintained graph family, scalar lag and
innovation law must be defensible before applying it. An unrestricted latent
model may leave the whole line admissible. In the opening pricing example,
the narrower set already contains opposite net values, so a more elaborate
estimator is useful only if its information or restrictions can resolve a
consequential ambiguity. A labelled whole-line result can be the correct
answer to a well-defined question.

\chapter{Correcting records can change the action}
\label{rewrite:observation}

A treatment record is a measurement of an event. Let $A$ be true randomized
receipt, $W$ recorded receipt and $Y$ gross contribution in pounds at a
fixed horizon. In this separate finite example, $P(A=0)=P(A=1)=1/2$
and $\E[Y\mid A=0]=100$, $\E[Y\mid A=1]=140$. Receipt is
randomized by construction; correcting its record would not establish
randomization in an observational campaign.

Suppose misclassification is nondifferential with a known matrix
\[
 K=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad K_{wa}=P(W=w\mid A=a,Y).
\]
Writing $p_a=P(A=a)$ and $q_a=\E[Y\mathbf1(A=a)]$, the recorded
shares and outcome moments obey
\[
 p_W=Kp_A=(0.55,0.45)' ,\qquad q_W=Kq_A=(59,61)' .
\]
Thus the recorded contrast is $61/0.45-59/0.55=28.2828\ldots$.
The matrix has determinant $0.7$, so its inverse recovers
$p_A=(0.5,0.5)'$ and $q_A=(50,70)'$, giving the true contrast
$70/0.5-50/0.5=40$. This is the moment version of the joint-law
argument in Chapter~\ref{r3:observation}. It is checked by direct
multiplication and solution, with no estimated audit law.

\section{The value of knowing the observation law}
At a stipulated action cost of \pounds35, the recorded comparison gives
net value about $-\pounds6.72$, whereas the corrected contrast gives
\pounds5. That reversal is conditional on the known error law. If an
identity matrix and the displayed matrix both remain admissible, the same
recorded shares and moments are compatible with different latent effects
and opposite recommendations. Reporting only the corrected number would
replace measurement uncertainty with a convenient assumption.

In a real validation sample, estimating $K$ would add uncertainty. The audit
must identify true receipt and represent the relevant customers and periods;
a classifier's own label is not an external truth measurement. Near-singular
matrices amplify error, and a singular matrix destroys recoverable information.
The retained chapter gives the symmetric-error example where receipt becomes
uninformative. More rows with the same deficient measurement law do not
restore its rank.

Entity linkage poses a related but distinct problem. A household may hold
several accounts, and a mistaken join can change both its treatment and its
outcome. Correctness counts alone may fail to identify the needed contrast;
the detailed linkage studies and their adverse results remain in this book.
The next useful observation is a correctly sampled, truthful linked history
when that is what the estimand requires, not merely a higher aggregate match
score. Likewise, event time, availability time and revision time must remain
separate when constructing a prospective decision view.

The four journeys now imply a common requirement for the proposed service.
It must keep the economic target and the information that identifies it
attached to the numerical result. Their statistical procedures remain
different: stratified assignment contrasts, sequential policy averaging,
model-set propagation and observation-law inversion. The next chapters
develop those differences before the software and investment synthesis chooses
which ones are ready for a bounded comparison.

\section{A fitted linkage analysis needs an external information budget}
Chapter~\ref{gap29:observation} studies a different observation problem:
matching randomized participants to outcomes when identifiers are corrupted.
It compares exact and fuzzy rules, keeps unmatched customers in the target,
and derives a contribution bound when at most a supplied number of candidate
lists omit the true match. Sampling uncertainty is then added under explicit
support and assignment assumptions. This is not an estimate of the receipt
matrix used above; the two studies concern different measurement mechanisms.

At 30\% outcome-dependent corruption, the robust population interval averages
119.1 outcome units in width, compared with about 4.1 for the fuzzy analysis.
The extra width prices justified ignorance. The corruption budget and outcome
support are external premises, not quantities learned from matching confidence.
A monetary decision first maps those outcome units and bounds into its own
expense equation. When the admissible set straddles that decision threshold,
an independently resolved audit sample can be more valuable than a forced
match. The detailed history and audit studies retain the further complications
of dependent records and uncertain audit truth.

~~~

~~~text
\chapter{What the evidence changes about the proposed service}
\label{rewrite:evidence-consequences}

The four journeys distinguish a wrong target, insufficient treatment support,
causal ambiguity and uncertain measurement. Those failures demand different
responses. A common service should make the distinctions visible while
reusing the appropriate statistical procedures. Its initial scope follows
from the evidence below; it does not require every possible capability to
be implemented at once.

\section{A result should change a design choice}
The existing 3,000-replication generated offer study is evidence about target
alignment. Under one specified design, the residual projection averages
26.447 when the equal-population benefit is 50. Its interval covers its own
target in 97.2\% of repetitions and the population target in none. At the
stipulated cost of 40, interpreting it as the population effect rejects the
beneficial offer in all 500 repetitions of that scenario. The design
consequence is to put the population weights and target in the result,
and to compare implementations only after aligning those quantities. A
more precise projection is not a repair for this interpretation error.

The separate 6,000-replication sparse-support study addresses inference
after the target is aligned. Pooling yields 94.7\% conditional coverage
under equal normal variances but 52.2\% under the tested unequal-variance
case. Cellwise Student intervals joined by a union bound preserve the
conditional coverage guarantee in the normal model at the cost of very
wide intervals. Thus the initial implementation should show cell support
and retain an unsupported or inconclusive result. If useful precision
requires unjustified pooling, the next expenditure should improve assignment
support or the information collected. These are existing generated
experiments, not evidence of superiority by a named external package.

The public UCI timing study answers a different question. On 41,188 archived
contact records, later-archive prediction has AUC 0.630 using the candidate
pre-call feature set and 0.793 when duration is added. The latter feature
is unavailable before the call, so its predictive gain cannot justify
pre-call targeting. Differences between early and late archive outcomes
also matter for evaluation. The correct service response is to preserve
availability dates and the evaluation period. Neither score estimates
the effect of making a call. Chapter~\ref{scisyn:evidence} gives the
executed design, comparators, results and qualifications.

The retained public 401(k), monetary, panel and linked-record analyses
provide further empirical and methodological context. Their sampling,
instrument, design and observation restrictions remain attached to their
results in the detailed evidence part. A working independent-observation
covariance in a public application does not validate a bank's common-calendar
uncertainty. A successful finite construction does not settle the unrestricted
linked-history problem. The negative findings remain relevant because
they identify the information a future bank study must supply.

The new one-sample deposit calculation in Chapter~\ref{rewrite:deposit}
completes the numerical route from estimation to contribution. Its callable
and command-line agreement tests the delivery of that particular report.
The four existing library/CLI/MCP cases test semantic consistency for
their own operations, including unsupported dependence. They establish
complementary facts. The later public experiment also carries fitted effect and covariance
summaries through all three interfaces (Chapter~\ref{gap29:public}).
Raw-data fitting and final reporting remain local scripts. These executions
are not a matched analyst trial, a general estimation service or evidence
of improved bank outcomes.

\section{Choose the smallest comparison that can reverse the recommendation}
The first comparison should take the same fixed offer question through
expert composition and a minimal shared integration. The cases should
include correct assignment, heterogeneous effects, unequal treatment
support, unavailable predictors, misrecorded receipt and a dependent
sampling request outside the accepted route. The generated law supplies
truth where that is possible; a public case supplies realistic data handling
without pretending its causal truth is known. A valid refusal counts as
a completed scientific answer when the information is insufficient.

An independent evaluator should judge target correctness, assumption
visibility, uncertainty, interpretation and avoidable errors. Time must
include correction, interpretation and unsuccessful attempts. The estimate
itself is not a success metric when its target differs from the request.
The proposed comparison is not yet an executed analyst study; its purpose
is to discover whether the common representation is worth its expense.
If both workflows reach equivalent answers at equivalent cost, improve
the existing workflow. If the integration reduces consequential errors or
repeated work, a narrow bank-data pilot becomes a defensible next step.
~~~

~~~text
\section{What the newer studies add to that choice}
The public earnings contrast tests the complete chain from observed rows to
uncertainty and an explicit spending hurdle. A positive contrast alone does
not establish that a cost is covered. The servicing comparisons show why a
fitted policy can offer narrow but misleading uncertainty when dropout or
state assumptions fail. The institutional panel separates persistent level
adjustment from a coherent economic unit; the linkage study makes the cost
~~~

## Edit 39

docs/writing-repair/2026-10-29/src/66540a8f29f1b949.tex

Assemble one authoritative treatment with all distinct supporting sections.

Before:
~~~text
\chapter{Choosing the capabilities worth assembling}
\label{scisyn:software}

A bank does not buy an average treatment effect. It buys a better decision:
which customers to contact, which price to quote, which branches to reorganise,
or which experiment to fund. Software is useful when its answer bears on that
decision and its assumptions are credible in the setting. A method that answers
a narrower question accurately can be more valuable than an ambitious system
whose output is difficult to interpret.

The detailed comparisons in this monograph support selective reuse. The first
proposal should assemble a small number of named statistical procedures around
a common description of the decision. It should retain a second implementation
where disagreement could expose a consequential mistake. It should not promise
to reproduce every package in one language. The development expense of such a
rewrite is certain; the benefit remains to be demonstrated.

The comparison below draws on the retained technical sources and their dated
versions. It is a synthesis of those inspections, not a new census of current
releases. Research coverage ends on 7 October 2026; acquisition after that date
does not establish historical availability of a mutable manual. A documented
procedure, an executed example and a proposed integration are different kinds
of evidence. Commercial tools are compared by their documented procedures;
unobserved functions remain unknown rather than being treated as absent.

\section{Discovering relationships and identifying effects}

\subsection{1. Discovery from independent observations}
For a cross-sectional customer study, the first choice is the set of assumptions
under which conditional independence or a score can reveal useful structure.
The inspected R pcalg, Python causal-learn and Java Tetrad implementations provide
concrete comparison routes for PC. They expose choices about independence tests,
search and orientation. Using the same algorithm name does not align those
choices. A graph with unresolved directions is a legitimate result, not an
unfinished diagram to be completed by managerial intuition.
\citep{exec13_pcalg_reuse_primary,v12_sw_causallearn,exec13_java_tetrad}

For the first restricted comparison, integrate one existing PC implementation
and retain another as a scientific comparator. Record the independence test,
sampling unit, significance level and treatment of orientation conflicts.
Porting the search into a new language is not justified by the proposal's
present evidence. Score-based, functional and continuous-optimisation methods
belong beside PC as different modelling choices, rather than votes for a
majority graph. In particular, agreement among bridges to the same underlying
engine is not independent corroboration. The software recommendation changes
if the bank needs a mixed-data model, hidden common causes or repeated records:
those needs require a separate statistical comparison before an interface is
chosen.

\subsection{2. Hidden common causes, selection and equivalent graphs}
An apparent connection between contact and repayment may arise because staff
recognise distress that the database does not record. Under such circumstances
an analysis assuming no hidden common causes can be precise about the wrong
model. The inspected discovery sources distinguish procedures such as PC and
FCI and different graph representations. An algorithmic orientation conflict
must not be reinterpreted as an established hidden common cause merely because
the display uses a similar pair of arrowheads.
\citep{v12_sw_causallearn,exec13_pcalg_reuse_primary}

The partially directed or ancestral graph determines a range of intervention
conclusions under its stated assumptions. A latent-variable route also needs
an explicit interpretation of its endpoints. Selecting one convenient
orientation would instead report an unidentified effect as identified. This is a rejection of an inference, not of a software
family. Where observationally equivalent models imply different lending
decisions, additional timing knowledge or experimental information is the
valuable purchase. Another graph visualiser cannot supply that information.

\subsection{3. Time, interventions and changing regimes}
Repeated customer observations contain both persistence and common shocks.
The retained Tigramite sources distinguish discovery methods, tests, lag
conventions, graph classes and effect calculations conditional on a supplied
graph. Their observation and masking rules matter when a calendar period is
missing. A row after a missing month is not necessarily the next economic
period. Commercial dynamic-network and structural time-series routes are
useful alternatives, but a supplied temporal model and a discovered model
answer different questions.
\citep{exec23_tigramite_reuse_source,exec13_ct_genie_dbn,exec13_ct_stata_svar}

Prefer restricted temporal integration that retains the original calendar,
observation availability and allowed intervention. Separate evidence from
multiple regimes from an assumption that one stationary regime describes all
years. A rate change during a funding crisis need not have the response seen
in ordinary months. Do not promise a general temporal effect from a lagged
prediction improvement. The first comparison should assess whether plausible
lag and regime choices change the decision, with graph ambiguity carried into
the effect calculation.

\subsection{4. Adjustment, identification and counterfactual questions}
The bank must distinguish identification of an intervention distribution from
evaluation of a structural model that somebody has supplied. Ananke's inspected
identification and model-oracle interfaces make this distinction concrete.
aGrUM and pyAgrum likewise combine graphical, symbolic and numerical facilities
whose individual meanings must be preserved. A symbolic expression may still
require conditional distributions unsupported by the observed population.
\citep{exec24_ananke_source,exec19_cxx_identification_source,exec24_agrum_source}

Symbolic identification determines what can be learned before an estimator
is selected. Model-based counterfactual simulation answers a separate question
conditional on the supplied structure. A simulation from that structure
therefore cannot establish identification from observational records.
An R, Python or C++ route is acceptable only if it preserves the query,
conditioning set, hidden-variable assumptions and support requirements. The
unresolved commercial comparison concerns exact query semantics and supported
model classes; a capability label such as causal analysis is insufficient.

\section{Estimating benefits from actions and repeated policies}

\subsection{5. Average and heterogeneous effects}
EconML's residual-regression formulation illustrates why the final effect model
matters as much as the prediction methods used to remove confounding. In a
binary-treatment setting with sufficient observed adjustment information $S$,
write $e(S)=P(A=1\mid S)$ and $\tau(S)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid S]$. With exact nuisance
functions and a constant final coefficient, the population projection is
\[
 \theta_* = \frac{E[e(S)\{1-e(S)\}\tau(S)]}
                   {E[e(S)\{1-e(S)\}]}.
\]
The average benefit for the target population is instead $E[\tau(S)]$.
These coincide under a constant effect, but need not do so otherwise. This
derivation concerns a restricted specification, not every EconML estimator.
\citep{exec19_econml_source}

An explicit specification separates adjustment variables, effect modifiers
and population weights before an existing estimator is used.
R forest and targeted-estimation routes and Python DML routes should be compared
on the same population and intervention, not on their default output names.
The inspected grf source gives a concrete R/native reference, while commercial
Stata CATE procedures provide an additional documented comparator.
\citep{exec13_grf_rpath,exec13_ch_stata}
The proposed service's contribution is to make these choices visible and
repeatable. It has not demonstrated predictive or causal superiority over the
existing estimators. The generated study in Chapter~\ref{scisyn:evidence} examines
the decision consequence of an omitted effect modifier.

\subsection{6. Experiments, instruments and discontinuities}
Eligibility rules, capacity limits and randomised offers can supply stronger
designs than adjustment alone. The inspected commercial IV manuals and
rdrobust sources provide useful estimation and diagnostic comparators.
Their identifying premises remain substantive: a valid excluded instrument
requires an argument about the outcome, and a discontinuity requires a
credible comparison at the threshold. Bias correction for an RD estimate does
not establish a strong first stage for a fuzzy design.
\citep{exec13_ivrd_stata,exec13_ivrd_sas,exec13_ivrd_rdrobust}

Integrate the design-specific procedure already used by the research team
before commissioning a general replacement. Match the threshold, bandwidth,
polynomial, kernel, treatment definition and uncertainty calculation in any
cross-language comparison. Preserve weak or uninformative conclusions. Reject
automatic conversion of an instrument coefficient into a portfolio-wide
effect without an argument connecting the relevant population. The first
investment is usually a better account of eligibility and assignment, not a
second two-stage least-squares solver.

\subsection{7. Longitudinal actions, survival and competing events}
A collections policy changes future customer condition and future treatment.
Adjustment for a condition caused by an earlier action can therefore change
the estimand. The retained R gfoRmula and Python pygformula implementations
provide inspectable simulation and resampling paths for specified longitudinal
interventions. Their histories, event ordering and competing-event options
must be compared explicitly. They are not equivalent to fitting a hazard
regression with a time-varying covariate.
\citep{exec20_gformula_reuse,exec24_longpy_pygformula_source,exec14_survival_sas,
exec14_survival_stata_competing}

Prefer a restricted integration of a complete longitudinal procedure. Retain
whole customer histories and state whether default, repayment, account closure
or death prevents the outcome being observed or is itself part of the outcome.
An intervention that eliminates a competing event is a different business
question from one that leaves it possible. Java and C++ survival components
can be useful computational ingredients, but the proposal does not infer a
complete sequential causal method from a survival routine. The unresolved
comparison is whether the entire policy, observation and uncertainty calculation
survives the chosen route, not whether it returns a plausible curve.

\subsection{8. Learning and evaluating a policy}
A policy assigns an action using information available at the decision date.
Choosing the best rule on historical outcomes and evaluating it on those same
outcomes rewards chance as well as merit. The inspected R policytree source
optimises supplied action scores; the sources for dynamic-regime packages
address different histories and decision sequences. A commercial offline
policy score or an optimum within a supplied decision model has its own
interpretation.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_policytree,exec24_policiesr_dtrreg,
exec24_policiesr_polle,exec16_cp_bayesfusion,exec13_ch_stata}

Use simple, prespecified policies as comparators before fitting richer rules.
Integrate score construction, policy search and independent evaluation as
separate steps. Restrict the action space when the historical policy supplies
little support, and report the customers for whom the recommendation cannot
be evaluated. Prefer native reuse of policy learners to an unmeasured rewrite.
Do not interpret the maximum historical score as the expected saving from a
bankwide policy. The useful next evidence is an out-of-sample value comparison
including action costs and the current decision rule.

\section{Changes across branches, markets and connected customers}

\subsection{9. Panel effects and staggered adoption}
The R did source distinguishes cohort, calendar, relative-time and treated-cell
aggregation. The inherited exact example has cohort shares $3/4$ and $1/4$;
the early cohort's effects are 2 and 4, and the late cohort's observed effect
is 10. The resulting aggregates are 4, $19/4$, 4 and $15/4$ for treated-cell,
group, dynamic and calendar targets respectively. None is an arithmetic error.
Their populations and time weights differ.
\citep{exec24_panelr_did}

Prefer a named group-time target and an explicit aggregation agreed with the
business owner. Compare R implementations with the inspected Python and
commercial panel routes only after matching the control population, treatment
timing, anticipatory period and uncertainty calculation. General fixed-effects
regression is an important comparator, not an automatic substitute for the
intended staggered-adoption target.
\citep{exec20_fixest_source,exec24_panelpy_differences,exec18_gp_stata_xthdid}
Missing cells can change the population; they must not disappear into an
unchanged label. Reusing an R or Python procedure through another language is
initially preferable to reproducing its entire aggregation and inference
logic around a generic regression solver.

\subsection{10. Synthetic controls and comparative time series}
For a small number of treated regions, donor suitability can matter more than
the choice of optimiser. The synthetic-control construction uses untreated
units to represent an otherwise unobserved trajectory under restrictions on
the outcome process and pre-intervention fit. Those restrictions need a
banking interpretation, including whether the proposed intervention affects
the donors.
\citep{abadie2010}

Retain synthetic controls as a distinct comparison alongside panel methods.
Document donor eligibility, outcome units, pre-period choice and the protocol
for uncertainty. The inspected Synth-for-Stata implementation is community
software hosted by a commercial product; licensing the host does not establish
vendor authorship or support for the extension. The R CausalImpact path is a
different model-based construction, with its own assumptions about controls
and stability.
\citep{exec19_synth_stata_source,exec13_ci_r,exec13_ci_semantics}
Adopt the complete documented route for a bounded study; defer a new port until
there is evidence of a material deployment advantage. The proposal should
compare sensitivity to donor and model choices before promising robust regional
savings.

\subsection{11. Dynamic panels, structural shocks and common calendars}
A branch balance equation can contain lagged balances, rates and common funding
shocks. Dynamic-panel instruments, structural VAR restrictions and local
projections address different questions. The inspected Stata and EViews sources
provide concrete commercial comparators; they do not establish that a branch
rate-setting policy is exogenous.
\citep{exec19_dynamic_stata_ab,exec19_dynamic_stata_system,
exec19_dynamic_stata_lp,exec19_dynamic_eviews_panel}

Integrate a model only with its instrument restrictions, horizon and sampling
unit. A large number of customer rows does not create a large number of
independent policy dates. Preserve the effective calendar and ask whether
uncertainty is driven by branches, common dates or both. Forecasting can be
valuable in its own right, but a forecast response to an input change does not
by itself justify changing a pricing rule. A new native implementation should
be considered only after the instrument and dependence comparison changes a
specific decision about the first prototype.

\subsection{12. Networks and spillovers}
Contacting one member of a household can affect another; a branch campaign can
shift business across nearby branches. The inspected MossSpider and
inferference sources implement different network and grouped-allocation
constructions. Their eligible populations, exposure definitions and uncertainty
calculations cannot be harmonised by renaming columns.
\citep{exec24_interference_mossspider,exec24_interference_inferference}

For an initial study, choose one economic exposure and one defensible assignment
mechanism. Preserve the population of outcomes separately from the population
of possible recipients. Integrate the matching statistical method and retain
a no-spillover analysis as a deliberately restrictive comparator. Generic Java
or C++ network libraries can represent relationships or simulate a supplied
process; that is not evidence that they identify an effect in the observed
bank network. Reject the claim that connectivity alone resolves interference.
The highest-value missing information is often the assignment mechanism and
the economically relevant links, not a faster graph traversal.

\subsection{13. Mechanisms, mediation and sensitivity}
A policy may improve repayment through contact, understanding and a revised
payment plan. The total effect of the policy and the effect of intervening on
one of those mechanisms are different quantities. The retained R mediation
paper explicitly distinguishes the additional assumptions needed for causal
mediation; randomising treatment alone does not settle them. The source also
distinguishes model and inference routes.
\citep{exec24_mediation_original,exec24_mediation_sources}

Adopt mediation procedures for a specified mechanism question, with sensitivity
analysis presented beside the estimate. Retain controlled and natural effects
as different interventions. A commercial mediation command is a useful
comparator only after the treatment, mediator, population and scale are aligned.
\citep{exec13_ci_stata_mediate,exec20_med_stata_multiple}
Reject an automatic decomposition of a predictive score as a causal mechanism.
For the investment decision, ask whether the mechanism would change what the
bank funds. If the same action is preferred across the credible sensitivity
range, a more elaborate decomposition may have little immediate value.

\subsection{14. Transfer, selection and missing observations}
Successful results from one branch need not transfer to another. Causal
transport requires assumptions linking the source and target populations;
filling missing values within the source population is a separate task.
The retained transportability argument and commercial imputation manuals
support this distinction.
\citep{pearltransport2014,exec21_transport_stata_mi,
exec21_transport_sas_mi_intro,exec21_transport_sas_mianalyze_intro}

Integrate imputation and target-population weighting as explicit, separately
justified operations. Report which outcome and assignment information is
missing and why it is believed recoverable. An imputed column does not recover
an unrecorded treatment policy or the potential outcome of a systematically
excluded population. Preserve adverse sensitivity results. Commercial systems
already provide substantial missing-data facilities; the proposed service's
candidate advantage is a clearer causal interpretation and repeatable
comparison, which still needs evaluation. No new universal solution to
unmeasured selection is claimed.

\section{Computation and the observations on which inference rests}

\subsection{15. Bayesian and hidden-state models}
Posterior computation is valuable when an economic model distinguishes hidden
credit condition from noisy observations. It quantifies uncertainty conditional
on the model and prior. It does not establish the restrictions that give a
policy intervention its meaning. The inspected Bayesian and factor-inference
sources therefore belong in a different category from observational graph
identification.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources,exec25_bsw_stan,exec24_libdai_source,
exec22_state_stata_bayesmh,exec22_state_stata_sspace_post}

Reuse a mature inference engine for a model that can be explained economically.
Keep prior sensitivity, convergence diagnostics, observation timing and
structural uncertainty visible. A posterior with narrow intervals can remain
conditional on restrictions the bank cannot verify. Prefer established R,
Python or C++ computation over a new sampler unless the model demands an
unavailable operation. Commercial graphical engines remain conditional
comparators, with numerical inference and causal identification assessed
separately.

\subsection{16. Identity, ownership and information dates}
Before a policy effect is estimated, records must represent the intended
customer, institution and decision date. The retained DuckDB, Feast and Polars
sources provide useful tools for queries, historical features and joins.
Their technical functionality cannot establish that a record was available
to a decision-maker merely because its economic event date is earlier.
\citep{exec19_duckdb_source,exec19_feast_source,exec23_polars_sources}

Adopt data-processing components, while retaining event time, publication time
and the time a corrected value became available. Validate ownership changes and
identity links against the particular target. A rare incorrect link can have
a large monetary consequence if it involves a large exposure. The existing
public-data survey makes UCI Bank Marketing useful for a timing example:
call duration is unavailable when deciding whether to place the call. It does
not establish an effect of calling from a representative untreated group.
\citep{pd15_uci_bank}
Reject retrospective access to later information in a purported historical
decision. The unresolved requirement is credible observation history, not a
missing SQL function.

\subsection{17. Numerical computation and a reproducible study}
Java regression libraries, C++ numerical kernels and other-language panel
packages can reduce development effort. Their statistical surroundings matter.
The inspected C++ panel sources sit inside procedures that select samples,
define effects and scale uncertainty; a coefficient solver alone does not
preserve those steps. A Julia suite and its individual components likewise
must not be counted as independent corroborating implementations.
\citep{exec25_paneljava_commons,exec25_panelcxx_fixest,
exec25_panelcxx_xhdfe,exec25_panelother_julia}

Adopt general numerical components where they answer a defined computational
need. Integrate complete statistical procedures when their sample and inference
rules are material. Port only after a measured constraint makes the expected
benefit exceed development, comparison and maintenance costs. A study run
through a library, a command line or an assistant should preserve the same
question and result. Agent frameworks and vendor service clients may help
conduct the work, but a completed call is not evidence that a causal
interpretation is justified.
\citep{exec24_framework_contracts,exec23_workflow_sasctl}

\section{What the commercial comparison changes}
Commercial statistical packages are credible alternatives, not an empty space
waiting for the proposed service. The inspected Stata procedures cover distinct
treatment, panel, survival and structural questions; the SAS sources distinguish
statistical procedures from service access. The bank may already possess
trained staff and relevant entitlements. A proposal that ignores those assets
overstates the saving from a new platform.
\citep{exec13_ci_stata_causal_intro,exec18_gp_stata_xthdid,
exec14_survival_stata,exec13_ivrd_sas,exec23_workflow_sasctl}

Compare three feasible alternatives: improve existing analytical practice;
connect a small set of existing procedures; or build a broader common service.
For each study, distinguish a vendor-authored procedure, a community extension
inside a commercial host, an open client to a licensed server, and a general
numerical component. They have different support and cost implications. The
comparison has not established exact current prices, complete entitlements,
performance at the bank's scale or the absence of equivalent features in all
competitors. Those are unresolved commercial questions, not findings of
technical superiority.

The proposed investment is therefore conditional. Its candidate contribution
is a disciplined connection between the business question, assumptions,
software choices and financial interpretation. Fund a narrow comparison that
can show whether that connection prevents material errors or saves analyst
time. If the existing estate achieves the same result more cheaply, retain it.
If differences in estimands, graph interpretation or information dates repeatedly
change decisions, a shared service becomes more persuasive.

\section{What remains to be learned}
The seventeen areas now lead to explicit provisional choices, but this synthesis
does not complete the underlying census. There is no claim that every
language--area pair has been exhaustively searched or that every candidate has
been executed. Complete dated source and capability comparisons where a missing
candidate could change the preferred route. Compare actual implementations on
matched questions before claiming numerical agreement. Obtain edition,
entitlement and price information before a purchase recommendation. Investigate
transitive numerical details only where they could change the inference or
the selected integration.

Some limits require new information rather than more programming: unidentified
effects under unrestricted confounding, absent support for a proposed action,
unknown assignment histories and uncertain transfer to a new population. State
the restrictions or data that would narrow each limit. These findings can
support a useful proposal even when they do not support a universal product.
~~~
